subChunks.title: Functional Interfaces & Lambda Syntax
subChunks.hookHtml: Imagine if you could hand a behaviour to a method — not just data, but a tiny piece of logic wrapped up and passed like a scroll. That is exactly what lambdas give you: concise, powerful expressions of behaviour that treat code as a first-class citizen.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Is a Functional Interface?

A functional interface is any interface that declares exactly one abstract method. That single contract is what makes it compatible with a lambda expression. The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended — it causes the compiler to enforce the one-abstract-method rule.

@FunctionalInterface
interface Greet {
    String greetings(String name); // only one abstract method
}

// Using a lambda instead of an anonymous class:
Greet g = name -> "Hello, " + name + "!";
System.out.println(g.greetings("Eldrin")); // Hello, Eldrin!

The Four Built-In Functional Interfaces

Java's java.util.function package ships four core interfaces that cover almost every situation:

// Predicate  — takes T, returns boolean
Predicate<Integer> isAdult = age -> age >= 18;
System.out.println(isAdult.test(21)); // true
System.out.println(isAdult.test(14)); // false

// Function  — takes T, returns R
Function<String, Integer> strLen = s -> s.length();
System.out.println(strLen.apply("Fireball")); // 8

// Consumer  — takes T, returns nothing (side-effect only)
Consumer<String> printer = s -> System.out.println(">> " + s);
printer.accept("Casting Frost Nova"); // >> Casting Frost Nova

// Supplier  — takes nothing, returns T
Supplier<String> randomSpell = () -> "Blizzard";
System.out.println(randomSpell.get()); // Blizzard

Lambda Syntax and Capturing Variables

Lambda syntax is flexible. Parentheses around the parameter are optional when there is exactly one parameter; curly braces and return are optional when the body is a single expression. Lambdas may capture variables from their enclosing scope only if those variables are effectively final (never reassigned after their first assignment).

// Various valid lambda forms:
Predicate<String> isEmpty = s -> s.isEmpty();      // one param, no parens needed
Function<Integer,Integer> square = (n) -> n * n;    // one param with parens
BiFunction<Integer,Integer,Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b; // two params

// Multi-statement body needs braces + return:
Function<String, String> shout = s -> {
    String upper = s.toUpperCase();
    return upper + "!!!";
};

// Capturing an effectively-final variable:
String prefix = "Spell: ";                   // effectively final
Consumer<String> tag = s -> System.out.println(prefix + s);
tag.accept("Arcane Bolt"); // Spell: Arcane Bolt

Method References (::)

When a lambda does nothing but forward its argument(s) to an existing method, a method reference is cleaner.

// Static method reference
Function<String, Integer> parse = Integer::parseInt;
System.out.println(parse.apply("42")); // 42

// Instance method reference on a particular object
String greeting = "Arcane Academy";
Supplier<Integer> len = greeting::length;
System.out.println(len.get()); // 14

// Instance method reference on an arbitrary instance of a type
Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase;
System.out.println(upper.apply("fireball")); // FIREBALL

// Constructor reference
Supplier<StringBuilder> sbFactory = StringBuilder::new;
StringBuilder sb = sbFactory.get();

storyBeats.text: Deep in the Arcane Academy's Lambdarium, rows of crystalline scrolls glow with distilled logic — each one a tiny spell of behaviour, waiting to be passed to whatever ritual requires it.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Welcome, apprentice. Until now you have passed *data* to your methods — integers, strings, objects. But true mastery begins when you pass *behaviour* itself. That is the gift of functional interfaces and lambdas.

storyBeats.speaker: Functional Interface
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice how the lambda replaces an entire anonymous class. Java's standard library provides four essential functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier. Learn these four and you can express almost any transformation.

storyBeats.speaker: The Four Core Interfaces
storyBeats.text:
Predicate<Integer> isPositive = n -> n > 0;     // test
Function<String,String> shout = s -> s + "!";    // transform
Consumer<String> log = s -> System.out.println(s); // consume
Supplier<Integer> roll = () -> 42;                // produce

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when your lambda merely calls a single existing method, use a method reference — the :: notation. It reads like a citation in a tome: 'use *this* method from *this* class.'
The apprentice studies the glowing scrolls, realising that lambdas are not just syntax sugar — they are a new way of thinking about code: behaviour as data, logic as values.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Cast three functional spells in a single Main class:

  1. Create a Predicate<Integer> named isGreaterThanTen that returns true if the number is greater than 10. Test it on 15 and 5, printing each result.
  2. Create a Function<String, String> named shout that converts a string to uppercase and appends "!". Apply it to "arcane" and print the result.
  3. Create a Consumer<String> named castingAnnouncer that prints "Casting: " followed by the string. Use it with "Fireball".
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier in your own words. Include: why would you choose one over another, and what does 'effectively final' mean when capturing a variable in a lambda?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank slate, write a Main class that does all three tasks without any starter code:

  1. A Predicate<Integer> testing whether a number is greater than 10 — test on 15 and 5.
  2. A Function<String,String> that uppercases and appends ! — apply to "arcane".
  3. A Consumer<String> that prints "Casting: " + the value — use with "Fireball".

rabbitHoleTerms.description: An anonymous function expressed inline, using the -> arrow syntax, that can be treated as an object implementing a functional interface.
An interface with exactly one abstract method, enabling lambda expressions and method references to be used wherever it is expected.
A functional interface whose test(T t) method returns a boolean — used for filtering and condition checks.
A functional interface whose accept(T t) method returns void — used for operations with side effects such as printing.
A functional interface whose apply(T t) method returns R — used for transforming a value from one type to another.
A functional interface whose get() method takes no arguments and returns T — used for lazy value production.
A shorthand for a lambda that simply calls an existing method, using the :: operator (e.g. String::toUpperCase).
A local variable that is never reassigned after its initial assignment; lambdas can capture effectively-final variables from their enclosing scope.

questions.prompt: Which built-in functional interface takes a value and returns void?
questions.explanation: Consumer<T> is designed for operations that consume a value and produce no result — its single abstract method is void accept(T t). This makes it ideal for side-effectful actions like printing or logging. Predicate returns a boolean, Function returns a value of type R, and Supplier produces a value without consuming one.

f.apply("magic") calls toUpperCase() on "magic" producing "MAGIC", then appends "!" to get "MAGIC!". p.test("magic") checks whether the length (5) is greater than 5 — it is not, so it prints false. Note the boundary: greater-than (strict), not greater-than-or-equal.

questions.prompt: This code fails to compile. What is the bug?
questions.answer: The variable 'prefix' is reassigned after its first assignment, so it is not effectively final and cannot be captured by the lambda.
questions.explanation: Java lambdas can only capture local variables from the enclosing scope if they are effectively final — meaning they are never reassigned after their first assignment. Here, prefix is assigned twice ("Result: " then "Answer: "), so the compiler rejects the lambda. The fix is to remove the second assignment, or copy the value into a new final variable: String p = prefix; and capture p instead.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct method reference equivalent of s -> s.toUpperCase()?
questions.explanation: String::toUpperCase is an instance method reference on an arbitrary instance of String. When used as a Function<String,String>, Java understands it as: for a given String s, call s.toUpperCase(). String::new is a constructor reference, System.out::println is a bound instance method reference on a specific object (System.out), and String::valueOf is a static method reference.

subChunks.title: Comparator and Sorting with Lambdas
subChunks.hookHtml: A Comparator is the arcane sorting rune of Java. With lambdas, writing custom sort orders becomes elegant — no more verbose anonymous classes, just clear, composable comparison logic that sorts your collections exactly the way you need.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Comparator Basics

The Comparator<T> interface has one abstract method: int compare(T o1, T o2). It returns negative if o1 should come first, zero if equal, positive if o2 should come first. Before Java 8, you'd write an anonymous class; now a lambda does the same job in one line.

List<String> spells = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Blizzard", "Fireball", "Arc"));

// Anonymous class style (old)
spells.sort(new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.compareTo(b); }
});

// Lambda style (modern)
spells.sort((a, b) -> a.compareTo(b));

// Method reference style (most concise)
spells.sort(String::compareTo);

Comparator.comparing() and Chaining

Comparator.comparing() accepts a key-extractor function and builds a Comparator from it. You can chain multiple sort criteria with thenComparing(), and reverse any Comparator with reversed().

// Sort by string length
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

// Sort by length, then alphabetically for ties
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
            .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));

// Reverse alphabetical
spells.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder().reversed());

// Using Comparator.comparing with a lambda key extractor:
spells.sort(Comparator.comparing(s -> s.substring(0, 1))); // first letter

Sorting Arrays and Custom Objects

Arrays.sort() also accepts a Comparator. When sorting custom objects, extract a field with a getter and pass it to Comparator.comparing().

String[] arr = {"Zap", "Arc", "Blizzard"};
Arrays.sort(arr); // natural order (alphabetical)
Arrays.sort(arr, Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)); // by length

// Custom object example:
record Spell(String name, int damage) {}
List<Spell> spellList = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
    new Spell("Fireball", 80),
    new Spell("Frost", 60),
    new Spell("Thunder", 90)
));
spellList.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Spell::damage).reversed());
// Now: Thunder(90), Fireball(80), Frost(60)

storyBeats.text: The Academy's Grand Sorting Hall is where apprentices learn to arrange their knowledge — spells catalogued by name, power, rarity. Without a Comparator, chaos reigns.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every collection must eventually be ordered. The Comparator is your sorting rune. In the old days, you'd write entire anonymous classes for a single comparison. Lambdas reduce that ceremony to a single expressive line.

storyBeats.speaker: Lambda Sort
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But the real power comes from Comparator.comparing() — it lets you extract a sort key cleanly. Chain thenComparing() for secondary sorts, and reversed() to flip the order entirely.

storyBeats.speaker: Chained Comparator
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Remember: Comparator is a functional interface. Any lambda with the signature (T, T) -> int is a valid Comparator. The standard library methods like comparing() are just convenient factory methods that build Comparators for you.
The apprentice sorts the Academy's spell registry in seconds — alphabetically, by power, by rarity — all with crisp, readable lambda expressions.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Sort the Academy spell registry two different ways:

  1. Create ArrayList<String> spells = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Blizzard","Fireball","Arc","Zap","Earthquake")). Sort alphabetically and print each spell on its own line.
  2. Sort the same list by length ascending (shortest first) and print each spell on its own line.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Arc appears first in alphabetical sort
Zap appears as a short spell in length sort

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain how Comparator.comparing() works in your own words. What does it mean to chain comparators with thenComparing(), and how is that different from writing a single complex lambda?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Recreate the sorting exercise from scratch — no starter code. Create the same list of 5 spells and sort it both alphabetically and by length, printing after each sort.

soloPracticeTests.label: Arc appears first in alphabetical sort
Zap appears as a short spell in length sort

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A functional interface for defining custom ordering; its compare(T o1, T o2) method returns negative, zero, or positive to indicate order.
A static factory method that creates a Comparator from a key-extraction function, making it easy to sort by a specific field.
A Comparator method that adds a secondary sort criterion, applied when the primary comparator considers two elements equal.
A Comparator method that returns a new Comparator with the ordering flipped.
The default sort order for Comparable objects (e.g. alphabetical for Strings, numeric for Integers), accessible via Comparator.naturalOrder().
An interface a class implements to define its natural ordering via the compareTo() method; distinct from Comparator which is an external ordering strategy.

options: A new List in reverse order
A Comparator with the ordering flipped
A Comparator that sorts by length descending
questions.answer: A Comparator with the ordering flipped
questions.explanation: reversed() is a default method on the Comparator interface that returns a new Comparator wrapping the original, with the comparison result negated. The original Comparator is unchanged (Comparators are typically immutable). It does not sort by any particular field — it simply mirrors whatever ordering the original Comparator defined.

Sorting by length ascending: Ox (2) < Cat (3) = Dog (3) < Elephant (8). So words.get(0) is "Ox" and words.get(words.size()-1) is "Elephant". The tie between Cat and Dog is resolved by the sort algorithm's stability (their relative order is preserved from the original list).

questions.prompt: This code throws an UnsupportedOperationException at runtime. Why?
questions.answer: List.of() returns an unmodifiable list, so calling sort() on it throws UnsupportedOperationException. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>() to get a mutable copy.
questions.explanation: List.of() creates an immutable list. Calling any mutating method on it — including sort(), add(), or remove() — throws UnsupportedOperationException. The fix is to wrap the list: new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)), which creates a mutable ArrayList initialised with those elements. This is a very common pitfall when using the factory methods introduced in Java 9.

questions.prompt: You want to sort a list of spells first by damage descending, then alphabetically for ties. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: The key insight is that reversed() reverses the entire comparator chain built so far, not just the next step. By calling .reversed() right after comparingInt(Spell::damage) (and before thenComparing), only the damage ordering is reversed. Then thenComparing(Spell::name) adds alphabetical as a secondary criterion in its natural (ascending) order. Option C reverses the whole final comparator — flipping both damage AND name order, which is wrong. Option D is not a valid API call.

subChunks.title: var, Text Blocks & Pattern Matching instanceof
subChunks.hookHtml: Java has shed its verbose reputation. Since Java 10 and 15, three quality-of-life features — local variable type inference with var, multi-line text blocks, and pattern matching instanceof — make code cleaner without sacrificing type safety.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
var — Local Variable Type Inference

Introduced in Java 10, var lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable from its initialiser. The type is still static and fixed at compile time — it just doesn't need to be written twice.

// Without var
ArrayList<String> spells = new ArrayList<>();

// With var — same type, less repetition
var spells = new ArrayList<String>();
var count = spells.size(); // inferred as int

var limitations — you cannot use var for:

  • Fields
  • Method parameters
  • Return types
  • Variables without an initialiser
  • Lambda parameters (well, you can in Java 11+ but it's unusual)

Text Blocks

Text blocks (Java 15+) let you write multi-line strings naturally with """ delimiters. Leading indentation is stripped automatically based on the closing delimiter's position.

String spellDescription = """
        Name: Arcane Surge
        Power: 95
        Element: Arcane
        Effect: Unstoppable magical force
        """;
System.out.println(spellDescription);

The content between the opening """ and closing """ is the string. Escape sequences still work. Trailing newlines are included.

Pattern Matching instanceof

Before Java 16, you needed to cast explicitly after an instanceof check:

// Old way
if (obj instanceof String) {
    String s = (String) obj; // redundant cast
    System.out.println(s.length());
}

Pattern matching combines the check and binding into one expression:

// Modern way — Java 16+
if (obj instanceof String s) {
    System.out.println(s.length()); // s is already a String here
}

// Works in a method:
static void classify(Object obj) {
    if (obj instanceof String s) {
        System.out.println("It's a String: " + s);
    } else if (obj instanceof Integer n) {
        System.out.println("It's an Integer: " + n);
    } else {
        System.out.println("Unknown type");
    }
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy's ancient scribes had copied the same type twice on every scroll — once on the left, once on the right, an exhausting ritual. A young reformist mage had petitioned for change for decades. Java finally listened.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: When the type is obvious from the right side, var spares you the redundancy. But do not abuse it — if var hides intent, write the type. Clarity beats brevity.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Text blocks end the era of concatenated strings. A spell description belongs on multiple lines — let it breathe. The compiler strips the leading indentation so your code can be properly indented.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And pattern matching instanceof eliminates the dance of check-then-cast. One line, one step, the variable is bound and typed immediately.

storyBeats.speaker: Code

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Three tasks in main:

  1. var: Declare three variables using var: a List<String> with Arrays.asList("Fire", "Ice"), an int as the list's size, and a String via String.join(", ", list). Print each.
  2. Text block: Create a text block with at least two named lines (e.g., Name: Arcane Surge and Element: Arcane) and print it.
  3. Pattern matching: Write a static method classify(Object obj) that prints "It's a String: " + s if the obj is a String, or "It's an Integer: " + n if Integer. Call it from main with a String and an Integer argument.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Prints text block content containing Arcane Surge
Prints It's a String for String argument
Prints It's an Integer for Integer argument

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what 'type inference' means for var — Java is still statically typed, so what exactly does the compiler do? Then explain why var cannot be used for method parameters, and what would go wrong if it could.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory: use var to declare a list of potion names and print its size. Write a text block with a potion label and effect on separate lines and print it. Write identify(Object obj) that prints "String detected: " + the value if String, or "Number detected: " + the value if Integer. Call it with both types.

soloPracticeTests.label: Prints String detected for a String argument
Prints Number detected for an Integer argument

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The compiler's ability to deduce a type automatically from context. var uses this for local variables; generics also rely on type inference.
var cannot be used for fields, method parameters, return types, or variables without initialisers. It is strictly a local variable feature.
Java strips indentation from text blocks based on the least-indented line (or the closing delimiter), so you can indent the block with your code.
A Java 16 feature where instanceof both checks and casts in one expression: if (obj instanceof String s) gives you s as a String directly.
The new variable introduced by a pattern match (the s in 'instanceof String s'). It is in scope within the true branch of the if statement.
Java 21 allows patterns with a 'when' guard: case String s when s.length() > 5 — combining pattern binding with a condition.
The formal process by which Java features are proposed, refined, and delivered. var was JEP 286, text blocks JEP 378, pattern matching instanceof JEP 394.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid use of var?
questions.explanation: var requires an initialiser on the same line so the compiler can infer the type. It cannot be used for fields (private var), return types, or without an initialiser. var items = new ArrayList<String>(); is valid — the type is inferred as ArrayList<String>.
"Hello" matches instanceof String s, and "Hello".length() is 5. The integer 7 matches instanceof Integer n, and 7 * 2 = 14.

questions.answer: var requires an initialiser on the same declaration line so the compiler can infer the type. Split declaration and assignment is not allowed. Fix: var message = "Hello, Academy!";
questions.explanation: var uses the initialiser expression to determine the type at compile time. If no initialiser is present on the declaration line, there is nothing to infer from, and the code fails to compile. Combine the declaration and assignment: var message = "Hello, Academy!";

questions.prompt: When should you prefer writing the explicit type instead of var?
options: Always — var reduces readability in all cases
When the right-hand side clearly shows the type (e.g., new ArrayList<>())
When the type is not obvious from the initialiser and a reader needs to know it
questions.answer: When the type is not obvious from the initialiser and a reader needs to know it
questions.explanation: var works best when the type is evident from context. When a method returns an opaque type (e.g., var result = processSpells(data)), the reader loses information. In that case, writing the explicit type aids comprehension. The guiding question is: does hiding the type hurt the reader?

subChunks.title: Sealed Classes & Switch Pattern Matching
subChunks.hookHtml: What if the compiler could guarantee you've handled every possible subtype of an interface — the same way it guarantees you've handled every enum constant? Sealed classes make that possible, and pattern matching instanceof ties the pieces together.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sealed Interfaces and Classes

A sealed interface (Java 17) restricts which classes may implement it. The permits clause lists every allowed implementor — no others are possible.

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}

record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Square(double side) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}

Because the compiler knows the exact set of subtypes, it can verify exhaustive handling — just like enums in a switch.

Pattern Matching with if-instanceof (Java 17 Compatible)

In Java 17, you can use chained instanceof pattern matching to dispatch on sealed subtypes:

static String describe(Shape s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c) {
        return "Circle with radius: " + c.radius();
    } else if (s instanceof Square sq) {
        return "Square with side: " + sq.side();
    } else if (s instanceof Triangle t) {
        return "Triangle base: " + t.base();
    } else {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Unknown shape");
    }
}

Switch Expressions with Pattern Matching (Java 21)

Java 21 (and Java 17 with --enable-preview) allows switch expressions over sealed types with pattern cases. The compiler enforces exhaustiveness.

// Java 21 style — shown for reference
String result = switch (s) {
    case Circle c    -> "Circle radius: " + c.radius();
    case Square sq   -> "Square side: " + sq.side();
    case Triangle t  -> "Triangle base: " + t.base();
}; // no default needed — sealed is exhaustive

Since the sandbox runs Java 17, use the if-instanceof style shown above for exercises.

Why Sealed Classes?

  • Express domain hierarchies that are intentionally closed
  • Enable exhaustive analysis by the compiler (and IDEs)
  • Pair naturally with records for algebraic data types
  • Prevent accidental extension from unrelated code

Sealed Hierarchy Rules

  • Every permitted subtype must be in the same package (or module)
  • Subtypes must be final, sealed, or non-sealed
  • Records are implicitly final, so they work perfectly as permitted types

storyBeats.text: The Academy's Shape Taxonomy had grown unruly — foreign scholars kept adding new shapes that the Core Spells weren't prepared to handle. Eldrin sealed the hierarchy, granting the compiler the authority to enforce it.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A sealed interface is a closed contract. You declare exactly which forms it may take. No outsider can slip in an unlisted subtype and break your handling code.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In Java 17, chain your instanceof pattern matches. The sealed contract is your promise that no else branch will ever be reached for a well-formed Shape.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In Java 21, the switch expression elevates this further — the compiler itself verifies exhaustiveness over sealed types, and the else is gone. Your code reads like the algebra it models.

storyBeats.speaker: Code

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
At the top of your file (outside Main), define:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Square(double side) implements Shape {}

Inside Main, write a static method describe(Shape s) that uses chained instanceof pattern matching:

  • If Circle: return or print "Circle with radius: " + the radius
  • If Square: return or print "Square with side: " + the side

In main, call describe(new Circle(5.0)) and describe(new Square(3.0)) and print the results.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what 'sealed' means in Java and why it is valuable beyond just good documentation. How does sealing a hierarchy change what the compiler can verify? Contrast with a regular interface that anyone can implement.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory: define a sealed interface Spell permits Offensive, Defensive with record Offensive(String name, int power) and record Defensive(String name, int shield). Write a cast(Spell s) method using instanceof pattern matching that prints "Attacking with [name] power [power]" for Offensive and "Defending with [name] shield [shield]" for Defensive. Call it with both types.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A Java 17 feature where a class or interface restricts which types may extend or implement it using the 'permits' clause.
A type defined as one of a fixed set of variants, common in functional languages. Sealed interfaces + records approximate ADTs in Java.
A switch expression where the compiler verifies that all possible values are handled — required for enums and (in Java 21) sealed hierarchies.
A modifier for a permitted subtype that reopens it for arbitrary extension, creating a mixed hierarchy of sealed and open branches.
A switch expression that can match on types and destructure records directly, with compiler-enforced exhaustiveness over sealed types.
Java 21 allows destructuring a record directly in a pattern: case Circle(double r) instead of case Circle c — then using c.radius().
The idea of using a switch to simultaneously check a type AND extract its components, enabled by combining sealed classes with record patterns.

questions.prompt: What does the permits clause in a sealed interface declaration specify?
options: The exact set of classes allowed to implement the interface
The module the interface belongs to
questions.answer: The exact set of classes allowed to implement the interface
questions.explanation: permits lists every class (or interface) that is allowed to implement (or extend) the sealed type. No other class may implement it — the compiler enforces this at compile time.

questions.answer:
Woof from Rex
Meow from Luna
questions.explanation: greet(new Dog("Rex")) matches the first instanceof branch, returning "Woof from Rex". greet(new Cat("Luna")) matches the second, returning "Meow from Luna".

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this sealed hierarchy?
questions.answer: Square is not listed in the permits clause of Shape, so it is not allowed to implement Shape. Add Square to the permits list: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
questions.explanation: Every implementor of a sealed interface must appear in the permits clause. Square implements Shape is a compile error because Square is not permitted. Fix: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}

questions.prompt: You are modelling JSON values: a value is either a JsonString, JsonNumber, JsonBoolean, JsonNull, JsonArray, or JsonObject — nothing else. Which design is most appropriate?
options: A regular interface that any class can implement
An abstract class with six concrete subclasses
A sealed interface with six permitted record implementations
questions.answer: A sealed interface with six permitted record implementations
questions.explanation: The set of JSON value types is fixed and closed — exactly the use case for a sealed interface. Each variant is a data carrier (ideal for records). The sealed hierarchy enables exhaustive handling in switch expressions and documents clearly that no other variants exist.
